utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone in this courtroom. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President and Your Honours, good afternoon. It would be appropriate if we can briefly address the Chamber at the end of the hearing today, perhaps for two or three minutes, regarding procedural matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I noted down two or three minutes. And I take it that these are matters that will require a response from the Prosecution as well, so better put down four to six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is possible. Perhaps necessary, perhaps not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will see. We first will have to deal with the documents in relation to the testimony of Mr. Karavelic. Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3728, a set of 26 maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, first Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, is that 26 maps or 27?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is, no doubt, 26.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... on one map.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am grateful, Mr. President. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence object to the tendering of the 26 maps for the following reason: First of all, these are maps that were pre-marked carefully by the Prosecution. We know that as a general rule, pre-marked maps, as such, are not admissible and we have seen that in these maps, everything was there already, and the witness could just confirm what was already there. So that seems quite particular. Now, the following point is that these maps seem quite artificial. They don't really correspond to real topographical, geographic maps. Their scale was not what it was, due to enlargement. As you have seen, it was very hard to find one's bearings on there, although I know the Chamber will manage to do so, because of the enlargement and because we have lost the scale. So that is the reason why we are asking your Chamber to reject the tendering of these maps, first because it was too prepared, too pre-marked first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I press the tender of the maps. I note that during cross-examination it was not put to the witness that any part of the confrontation line was incorrect and given that the accused would well know the confrontation lines, it can therefore be safely assumed that the confrontation lines, as corrected by the General, are, in fact, correct. In relation to the other information on the maps, the position of the victims of the various incidents, that is the point of impact of the bullets and the shells, there is evidence before the Trial Chamber to cover that and likewise in relation to the source or possible sources of fire. In other words, everything in the map is now the subject, each of the maps, is now the subject of evidence. As to the basis that the maps are difficult to follow, I do not understand that submission. It was not suggested to the witness or to the Trial Chamber that there was any aspect of the maps that could not be followed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President I have to oppose what has just been said. I clearly said to your Chamber, I don't know, when I don't have the reference, because I believe that I was taken aback here. I said to the Chamber, be careful, take care of the scale. These maps are not usable as such and today this is a quite large obstruction. We are challenging a map per se. We haven't done it, but we did mention the scale. I wanted to mention that the HQ maps, the Main Staff maps that we produced, even these maps were rejected by the witness as having been made by people who were not professionals. That is where we stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although it seemed to be a rather different issue. It was the markings on the map, rather than the maps themselves that the witness said might have been done unprofessionally. But, Mr. Ierace, may I ask you one thing: Questions have been put in respect of the confrontation lines that were pre-marked, especially the witness was asked whether they were drawn correctly. So to that -- in that respect Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I am a bit surprised to hear that everything was there already, because the question was whether it was there correctly or not. But, you also noticed, Mr. Ierace, that the Chamber did not allow to ask any questions on, at least not on potential sniper positions since the Chamber was of the view that the witness had had ample opportunity to look at it, so that it might have contaminated his recollection, if he would have had any. Nevertheless, you, it seems, the Prosecution seeks the full information that contains of the maps to be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I would regard that as a separate issue. One issue being whether the information on the map is in accordance with the various victims, the police officers and so on. The second and separate issue is whether the witness was able to give independent evidence which was open to contamination because of the pre-markings on the map. So I would respectfully submit to you that the ruling of the Trial Chamber on that second issue is quite separate and does not affects the admissibility of that information. If anything, it explains the -- it demonstrates the basis of the Trial Chamber's decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will give a decision after this or the next break, but at least soon on the admission in evidence and whether it will be a full admission or whether after. So, Madam Registrar, these 26 maps, a decision will follow. Then, we are about to --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3644.VK3, map; Exhibit P37 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to just ask which map this is. Could I have more precise information regarding which map this is. May I ask if I can confer, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it is a pre-marked map, so the rule is not as general as --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the reason why we conferred, knowing that it was a pre-marked map, in order not to waste time for anyone. That's why we decided not to raise an objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P3644.VK3 is admitted into evidence

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P3727, series of five maps, marked by witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's then admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3735, B/C/S, receipt on temporary confiscated personal effects, P3735.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we did not receive this document in English. Is that a translation or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we received it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says English translation and it starts with "Collective Shelter Centre."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Ierace let me know when he forwarded it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think at the very moment of providing the document, but if there is another --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will focus on the translation, but perhaps we could leave the question for now, perhaps I could let you know about our position a little later on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would tell us whether there is any objection, perhaps later today, then, especially, then in respect of the translation. The original would not be objected by the Defence? I mean,--

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The original will probably be all right, but the translation could raise problems. But because I haven't had the opportunity, I will have a look at it now and I will let you know. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the B/C/S version and that is number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence and a decision will be taken on the translation into English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P3736, receipt dated 09/05/1992, signed by Vahid Karavelic in B/C/S. P3736.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it the same is true for the original and B/C/S is it needs no objection and the translation still has to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether we received the translation, but apparently not. I don't know whether we have had the translation or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I considered it more or less to be one document, but it is a second page --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we received it now, yes. Thank you. So same position, yes. Thank you. Mr. President, regarding the English translation of the first document that we received, I can already say that this is now -- I can say that, as usual, there are errors here and I am very surprised that the Prosecution can make such a mistake. When you see the original in Serbian, you can see very well that "Mitrovica" has been added in hand and it hasn't even been translated in English. So either we translate everything, or it has only been done partially. I will have a look at it in its entirety and will let you know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would give your comment on the document as a whole and we see that a part is stricken out and the handwritten addition is not added in the translation. Next document would be, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D143, certification dated 12 July 2002; D143.1, English translation; D144, B/C/S, decision from Presidency, dated 18 August 1992, Sarajevo; D144.1, English translation; D145, order Sefer Halilovic, dated 09 October 1992 in B/C/S; D145.1, English translation; D146, order dated 12/12/1993 in B/C/S; D146.1, English translation; D147, order dated 02 October, 1993; D147.1, English translation; D148, order dated 18 September 1993, D148.1, English translation; D149, order dated 16 February 1993; D149.1, English translation; D150, order dated 3 April 1994 D150.1, English translation; D151, report situation in zone of responsibility for period from 11 January to 12 January 1993; D151.1 English translation; D152, order 25/10/1993; D152.1, partial English translation; D153, document in B/C/S containing various maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. But since it was a little swift and we were not able to follow it, what we said for the 26 maps in relation to sniping incident, is the same position that we are stating for the five maps regarding the shelling incidents. The objection that we formulated is exactly of the same type for those five maps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to that, I would simply make the observation that the Defence is inconsistent in not objecting to Exhibit 3644.VK3, because that was not only pre-marked, but pre-marked with the assistance of others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to respond, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you don't want to. May I ask one question in relation to D Exhibit 153. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I cannot read everything that is on the first page of that document, but it seems to relate to a time period between the 1st of December 1992 until the 4th of April 1993. At the same time, on the second page, I find entries which reads, 13/06/1993, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Mr. President. That is correct. I noticed it and I believe that the very last addition was made afterwards, after the dates were put on the maps. So the first note is less precise than the key itself, which gives a more precise chronological scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say that someone must have forgotten to change the front page, perhaps, and yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably. Someone probably didn't add these differences because the previous key of the 8th of January 1993 seems to be covered by the latest date, which is the 4th of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the reason why, among others, I had photocopied the key so that it was possible to see that there was a problem with the date, that could be raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the second problem with the key is, I noticed on the original that there are nice colours on the key and nice colours on the map. Would there be one way or another to provide the Chamber at least with even where it just for these portions with a coloured version as well and perhaps the Prosecution as well, so that we at least are able to read what is in front of us, which it is totally impossible --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I will do it. The idea was to go through the witness and raise dates, but you can see that the witness rejected the map as having been made by someone who is incompetent. But we will make copies in colour so that we can give coloured copies to the Chamber and to the Prosecution. It will not happen immediately, but very soon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to the tender of the Defence documents the only one that I would object to is the purported certificate in relation to the prison. The Defence relied on that document in order to directly contradict the witness's claim, that he had been brought before a court in Belgrade. I object on the basis -- on two bases. Firstly, the certificate purports to only relate to his detention. It makes no comment as to whether he was tried in Belgrade. Secondly, even in that respect, it does not name the prison where the search was carried out. Indeed, it does not even identify whether there is only one military prison in Belgrade because "A" or "the" is missing for the reference to the military prison. Therefore, my objection is that the document relates -- the document does not have any probative value. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. I think we will have to -- yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence just wanted to respond to the objection of my learned colleague, moreover, because the certificate was issued by the military court which was the only one competent in this area, which was the only one that could have tried Mr. Karavelic. The reason why the Defence would like to have this document admitted is because Mr. Karavelic had said that he had been tried and he had been sentenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is exactly my point. The document does not say he was not tried, it does not say he was not sentenced. It simply says he was not detained at some unknown, unstated prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Karavelic stated that he had been convicted in the situation when he provided the statement, and when he said that he had been convicted, that means that in the period from the 28th of April until the 9th of May, that he was subject to a court proceedings and that he was convicted. And this is the reason why we are providing this certificate in order to show that he was not brought into custody nor was he serving a sentence in the military investigative court in Belgrade. That would be the only institution which could have tried Mr. Karavelic and kept him in gaol. From the certificate which the Prosecution provided, it is evident that he was in the collection centre in Sremska Mitrovica. So that was the document that does not show that he was taken into custody, nor that he was brought before a court, or that he was sentenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the parties seem to disagree. We will have to take a decision on the objection. We also will do that after the break. We will take the appropriate time to decide. I think we dealt with all of the documents by now, Madam Registrar. Just to inform the parties, it might be that a lot of objections all might have been made, that we even may take until tomorrow, and that there is nothing urgent at this very moment, so that we can better read your objections and better prepare our decision. Then, Mr. Ierace, may I take it that the Prosecution is ready to call its next witness which --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That will be Ewa Tabeau taken by Mr. Stamp. Might I be excused for the last 15 minutes or so in order to be present for the matter to be raised by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort expert witness Tabeau -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to simplify the work of the Chamber, the two English translations that were given, handed over to us, are almost acceptable. The only thing that I have indicated is the point that I raised on the first document, on the first page, there is a word missing which you will find in the original text. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Tabeau. Before giving evidence before this Chamber, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, please be seated. Ms. Tabeau, we usually all put on our headphones, because there might be interruptions in a language that you don't understand. Perhaps you do understand all languages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it would be preferable for you to have your earphones on. You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you begin by stating your full name?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: My name is Ewa Maria Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what is your occupation, could you tell us briefly?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I am a demographer. My professional educational background is statistics and econometrics. I graduated in 1981 in Poland from Warsaw School of Economics and started working shortly afterwards first in a small research institute at Statistics Poland, later, one year later at the Economic University of Warsaw.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. We could probably get to that in more detail, but could I get you straight to the point. Did you conduct some research into the casualties which occurred in the city of Sarajevo during the period of 1992 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. We completed a project in which we produced certain statistics, related to the city of Sarajevo in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you in charge of that project?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I was in charge of this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were the -- could you tell us the names of the major persons involved in this project.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down and pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, may I also ask you to make a brief pause between the question, before starting the answer. Otherwise, the interpreters will have difficulty in following you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I put it this way, did Marcin Zoltkowski and Jakub Bijak --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before interfering, I first heard no. Please tell me what you have to say. That could never start with the word, no. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Mr. President. I was saying no which was a say of saying that we were saying no to this kind of questions and this is the kind of question we would like to object to. Easily, this was a leading question phrased directly in this way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, if you want to object Mr. Piletta-Zanin the usual way of doing this is saying "I object to the question for these and these reasons," and not saying, "no." The second issue is, is it in dispute, could we reasonably expect that witness would be given the answer of those she would work with together because Mr. Stamp indicates these names? I mean, objection against leading questions are taken seriously, but should not the objection against the leading question be taken seriously as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. The Defence is objecting for the following reason: Is that it doesn't know the names of the persons that could have been associated with this study, with this report, and in terms of experts, the Defence has had very important things hidden from it and that is the reason why the Defence is not tolerating leading questions any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, on page 3736, the title page of this report, doesn't it mention three names?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because what you just said is that the Defence doesn't know the names of the persons that could have been associated with this study, with this report, in terms of experts, and the Defence has very important things "hidden" from it. I thought that you were asking for these names, Mr. Stamp, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I was trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, having heard the reasons for your objection, I fully do not understand it and it sounds rather frivolous.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it may happen that there will be other names that will be mentioned and that is the reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then wait until these other names might come up and then make an objection, but not the way you did it. This time you not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. using the time -- of the Prosecution to its case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am grateful, Mr. President. Perhaps I could do it this way. With your leave, Mr. President, could I show to the witness the document designated Exhibit P3731A which was filed on the 14th of May, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does that document contain a summary of your professional qualifications and experience?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And does it also contain a summary of persons who worked on this project under your -- I beg your pardon. May I withdraw that. Does it also contain a summary of the professional qualifications of persons who worked under your supervision on this project?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It also contains professional qualifications of the co-authors of this report, and this is Marcin Zoltkowski and Jakub Bijak. There were also other persons working on this project with me who are not the authors of this report, but these were people who were giving us different types of technical support in the course of the project. They are not mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the document now be taken and could the witness now be shown the document designated Exhibit 3731.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I take it that this document is the same one that we had before, the report, had this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Except that it has one more page, 118, but it is a blank page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the blank page bears no number, which is the second page of the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I am correct, that we are referring to a blank page at the end of the document? May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, it has been copied from --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Double-sided and reproduced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And on every page which is not there -- is nothing written on the back of the page, that we get a blank page for that. And also at the very end, one numbered blank page which is numbered -- numbering at the bottom of the page is 118 which is very much empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The original that I have -- has the same page blank, so don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am informed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everything is clear now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May we have that copy back, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing that could create some confusion, Mr. Stamp, is that this empty back page, 118, bears no number at the top, so, therefore, for the Registry, it will certainly create problems, but not for the Chamber at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you Madam, tell us what that document is in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is our report that is titled as mentioned in this document, "Population Losses in the Siege of Sarajevo, 10 September 1992 to 10 August 1994." It is the demographic report we prepared for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And does it contain six annexes?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU

utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what was the primary source of that and information that you used for your research and project?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We used several sources. The primary, the most important source was the Household Survey, Sarajevo 1994, which is a survey conducted by a group of academics in mid-1994, in Sarajevo. Actually, it was during the conflict and the situation was certainly not normal at that time in Sarajevo. But despite all difficulties, this group prepared a very large survey and conducted the survey, ultimately, 1994, and complete a huge quantity of information that could be used for a report like this one that we are presenting today to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the area of the survey or covered by the survey?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The survey -- perhaps, I will begin by saying that the survey was prepared by, I say it, academic professor, affiliated at the Sarajevo University. They actually spent several months on developing a survey questionnaire and preparing all procedures necessary to conduct such a huge survey. It was meant to be -- it is like a census population, census like a complete survey in which they would collect information from every household living at that time in the free territory of Sarajevo. By the "free territory" they understand the area within the confrontation lines, within the front lines as was set up by mid-1994. The survey was discussed with statistical authorities who were still active in Sarajevo to a certain extent at that time. And finally was conducted by help, with help of local communities in Sarajevo. As I said, it was, the survey was meant a complete population survey. Every household planned to be reached by the survey interviewers. I know from the director of the research institute who prepared the survey questionnaire and later took the responsibility of the survey, Professor Cekic, that they distributed 120.000 questionnaires, knowing that every questionnaire was meant for one household, this gives us a huge population of more than 300.000 individuals who actually were living in Sarajevo at that time and who were planned and finally largely were asked questions from the survey questionnaire. The survey was conducted with help of local communities, I said, from Sarajevo, from areas within the confrontation lines. Local communities are small administrative areas. We included a list of local communities that were participated, they participated in the survey, in end of our report. This is annex number 1, I believe. In annex 1, page 52, there is a list of local communities that were covered by the survey and these local communities, the staff working in this local communities actively engaged as survey interviewers, in collecting the information from the households. On the list, we see 89 local communities. This is, at the same time, this list must be seen as a survey area, as the area within the front lines, the free territory of Sarajevo. This is the expression used by the authors of the survey, not mine, the expression. This is the territory which was accessible to the survey interviewers, where they could reach the households, people living in the town, in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of the institute --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I know that there was a scientific board responsible for the substance and all also technical organisational aspects of the survey. This board consisted of a number of academics, a number of professors who at the same time, some of them were engaged in some other activities. The ethnicity of this group who was mixed, so there were Muslims, Serbs, and one Serb, actually, as far as I remember, and some Croats in the board. And I believe that the authors of the survey made a lot of efforts to ensure that there wouldn't be any bias related to the ethnic composition of the population covered by this survey. They made a lot of effort to reach also minority groups. We know that the Muslim population was the minority group in Sarajevo, before the war, and most likely during the war. But it was one of important aspects of this survey to reach every ethnic group, not only the Muslims living in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You attached a copy of the questionnaire used in the survey in annex 2. Could you comment on the quality, in terms of statistical science of the questionnaire which was used?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The questionnaire is attached here in two versions, one is the original B/C/S version. It is attached in annex 2, page number 56 and 57. This is the B/C/S version. And next we attached also the translation of the questionnaire, pages 58, 59. From these two pages, I will be, of course, focussing on the English version of the questionnaire, on the translated version. I said that the survey was meant as a population census, but the questionnaire cannot be seen as the one that is usually used in population census. The question in census are much more complex, longer. There are many items that are related with each other. This is a short and simple questionnaire. We have questions related to personal details of the person who is being questioned here: Name of the person, address, some questions about moving, whether the person moved during the conflict period or not. We have questions related to demographic events, important demographic events related to the conflict. We have question related to the killed persons, wounded persons to persons who actually were detained during the conflict, invalids and handicapped because of the conflict, live birth, still birth, some information about housing, type of housing, conditions in the house. And finally, last question related to a completely different issue, to victims or persons who suffered during the Second World War unrelated to this conflict we are discussing in our report. The questionnaire is short as compared with questionnaires used in censuses. It is simple. Questions are formulated very obviously. Especially I know from colleagues with whom I worked in the B/C/S version. So there is -- it was not difficult, I believe, to understand the questions. In addition to the questionnaire, every household received an explanation of the questions. So from the explanations, they could see, they could learn even more about the intentions of the authors of the survey, what type of information was to be collected and all related details were addressed in this additional document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, would you say that a survey of this -- sorry -- a questionnaire of this type - notwithstanding that it is not of the same length as one that would normally be used in a population census - would it be adequate or inadequate for the purposes of the project to study casualties during the period 1992 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Generally, it is very good that the questionnaire is rather short. Respondents are more likely to respond properly to short questionnaires and simple questions than to questionnaires which are complex and long. So I think for this type of survey and this type of material that we used in our demographic report, it is actually very good that it is a short and relatively simple questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you give us a brief overview of the work done to sort the results of this survey into it a database for your scientific project?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We -- as I said earlier, the authors of the survey distributed 120.000 questionnaires. They collected back approximately 85.000 questionnaires. So that is a certain degree of nonresponse, which is normal in every survey. This degree, about 30 per cent, is relatively low, if you think of the period, the situation in Sarajevo, but generally in every survey of this type, not regular census, but just a survey, this type of nonresponse, it is fairly acceptable. We, of course, did not computerise all material, available material, because it is a huge quantity of questionnaires, 85.000. We selected a number of questionnaires from the original material. Only those questionnaires were events like killing, wounding, and some personal information about the respondents were selected and computerized. We ended with a database in which we had approximately 40.000 records. And these records were records of killed and wounded persons, altogether, these are complete material, survey material. It is not what is -- all these records, the 40.000 are not necessarily are relevant to the indictment period and indictment area. But in the first step, we selected a number of questionnaires, all events reported, killing and wounding, and computerised everything. Then starting from there, we cleaned the information. We excluded records that were incomplete or wrong, unrelated to the indictment period, indictment area. And in that, with a database which is discussed here in this report and this database includes less records, of course.

This is a person that was either killed or wounded. In this database we have only persons who experienced these two types of events. In the beginning we had 40.000, approximately. It was more than that. We, after eliminating duplicates from this database, we ended with 37.057 records, which then we checked from the point of view of the period and area when they occurred. In this study, we used 20.151 records. Here, in this column, we see an overview of how many wounded persons, how many killed persons, and how many natural deaths are included in this database. These records are all related to the period from 10 September, 1992 to 10 August, 1994 in the area, the cover is the area within the confrontation lines, front lines, in Sarajevo as seen by mid-1994. So for the wounded persons we see 12.919 records; killed persons 3.798; and in addition to all these extraordinary deaths, we see a number of natural deaths which is 3.433 records.

Cause of death is an important indicator which allow -- which helps, makes it possible for us to distinguish between violent deaths or conflict-related deaths and natural deaths. So without having natural deaths in our database, we wouldn't be able to estimate the number of killed persons. So we didn't study natural deaths as such, but we included these records in order to be able to distinguish between conflicts-related, violent deaths and natural deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your report you speak of linking. Can I ask you to explain how one could confirm the accuracy or reliability of these records of the database by linking or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We did speak about linking or in other words, matching records with each other, records from different sources. What does this mean? Linking or matching is generally looking for information about one, the name persons, and the person is reported -- why the person is reported in different sources of information. Next to the Household Survey Sarajevo 1994, we used several other sources of information. About killed persons, for instance, we used the business records of the Bakija Funeral Home. This is the same type of information, deaths. We also used a source called Mortality Database, established by the Muslims Against Genocide, an organisation operating in Sarajevo. Again, this is the same type of source, information about killed persons is reported in this source. We also used other sources about surviving population. We used population census 1991, population census. We also used a list of others, just to confirm whether a person survived or indeed died during the conflict. By linking, we mean matching or linking information about the same persons from one source reporting deaths, with the population census. These are the two different sources, population census on one hand, a source like Sarajevo Household Survey on the other hand. Linking is important in this case, because population census is a complete population survey. Every person who lived at the time of survey in Sarajevo is reported in that census. So if you -- if we are able to find a given person, reported as death, for instance, killed or naturally died, in household, Sarajevo Household Survey, if we are able to find this person in the population census, we can be sure that this is a real person, that this person, indeed, lived in Sarajevo before the conflict started, and this way we can just confirm the identity of that person. So matching plays a very important role. It is just a confirmation of identity and actually, also a way we can show to what extent the source we use in analysis, in our analsis is reliable. So this is why linking is a very important part of our analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having done the linking or as you call it matching, with these various sources, did you come to a conclusions to reliability of the results of the Household Survey, Sarajevo 1994?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We obtained matcing rate, approximately 81 per cent, which is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relatively high. On higher matching rates can be only obtained for sources in which "maticni broj," personal identification number is included. For instance, in the voters register such a number is included, then the matching rate can be even higher than 80 per cent. It was not the case with Sarajevo Household Survey. So obtaining the matching rate higher than 80 percent, 81 per cent is actually very good. It is a good indicator of the reliability of this source.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now you referred to a variety of sources, which you collected data from for your studies. Are there sources, all of them exhaustive and if they are not, are they large enough to support a study of the nature of the one you conducted?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the sources about killed or wounded person are never exhaustive because this is a very special event, being killed or wounded, and the event occurs always in a conflict situation, not under peace. It would be very unusual to possess complete information, complete sources, about these types of events. So, the sources that we used for this report are all incomplete, but one of them, Household Survey, 1994 is very very large. It was meant to be complete, that it is not complete is because of the special circumstances that actually were there at that time. But the number of distributed questionnaires, collected back 85.000 questionnaires, gives us a total population of we estimate 340.000 individuals, which is a very large population. And we remember that this population which is about 70-75 per cent of the prewar population of the whole Sarajevo, in terms of six complete municipalities. So this is the area we are speaking about is not six complete municipalities, only part of the six municipalities. So this gives us a very large population in this area. Close to being complete, in my view. So the completeness, I would say, of the major source used for this report is rather high.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "only part of the six municipalities in Sarajevo," which part are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I am referring to the part within the front lines, which was the survey area, and we know that this area consisted of six municipalities, but not entire municipalities, only parts of each of the six municipalities below to the area that we call "within front lines area."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Household Survey, Sarajevo 1994, was conducted on the basis of the use of questionnaires. And I take it that there may be a possibility of double reporting of events which you described as woundings or killings, for the purpose of this survey. Could you briefly describe to us what procedures yourself and your team adopted in order to remove duplicates, if any?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Duplicates are always present in this type of sources. Why? Because the reporting is different than is usually done in normal times. We collect information about demographic events, in vital statistic system, normally, we say. The population has the obligation to report vital events like death or birth, to vital events office. These events are then registered officially, and this information is later used to compile aggregate statistics, numbers of births, deaths, marriages, divorces. We deal here with a survey in which respondents were just asked by interviewers to report certain events. They didn't have the obligation to prove that these events indeed occurred by showing, for instance, death certificate to the interviewers or a different document, legal official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just ask you to slow down a little bit for the record.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I am sorry. So when respondents are asked, the report events the way they remembered them. Moreover, certain households can repeat certain information about the same events and why? Because respondents sometimes don't understand what is the difference between a household and a family. Household sometimes is a different thing than a family. People tend to remember deaths in their family, than deaths in their household. Household is just a small unit that lives together and shares house and food. And families are -- can live in different places and not necessary share the house and the food with each other. So, certain events like death, which is a very important event in people's life, can be reported by different people and in this way, the same information about the same event is reported in a database twice or even more times. We always check for duplicates, we correct, we eliminate duplicates from our databases. We do this using information about persons. In section 3.3 of our report, I refer to page -- I am referring to page 13, 13, of the report, section 3.3 is titled "Duplicate Removal." We described in this section what has been done to eliminate duplicates. In brief, we compare records within the database use a number of criteria. Here in the last paragraph at the bottom of this page, the criteria or items say from the database are listed. We compare first name, last name, initial of father's name and year of birth. This is first -- very first step. A number of records had been removed once we applied this criterion, more specifically, we removed 2.798 records from the database. After having compared all records from point of view of the criteria, of the items I have mentioned. In the second step, we actually used similar items in our comparison, in our check for duplicates, last name and year of birth, but only three first letters of a first name. This is because of possible spelling mistakes in the names. To find as many duplicates as possible, we just restricted our search only to the first three letters of the first name. And here we had found 338 records that had been removed from the database. We continued our set for duplicates in the matching process. And during the matching process we had found another 15 duplicates that had been removed from the database. All these checks discussed in these sections must be seen as automatic procedures that can be applied by running certain programs through the database. In addition to this automatic checks, we searched for duplicates manually, and this is described to the addendum to the demographic report, where the checks were based on even more fussy criteria, like a certain percentage of contractors to be identified in compared records.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: More what type of criteria?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Fussy criteria. It is that only we specified a percentage, more specifically 75 per cent of characters in the name had to be identical in the records in order to list them as possible duplicates. This type of criterion implies that later, once we have a list made, we must go through the duplicates, probable duplicates and compare every two records with each other to see whether these are indeed duplicates or not at all. This again because of the spelling mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that there were two lists of duplicates, of possible duplicates from the final procedure adopted to find duplicates. Well, I think the title speaks for itself. These were the lists that were created from that final process of searching for duplicates?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The list attached with the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. These are the lists of possible duplicates, but we actually are unable ourselves to indicate whether we deal with duplicates or different persons. It is that we would need more information about persons in order to be 100 per cent sure that the persons indicated, listed in the addendum are the same persons. So only on the basis of first names, father's name, last name, and the date of birth and the date of event, it is sometimes very difficult to say whether the event, death or wounding, occurred to the same person or to two different persons. We tried to indicate a number of duplicates that we thought were 100 per cent duplicates. And I -- we discussed these numbers in the addendum in section 2 -- in section 2, generally searching results separately discussed for killed persons and wounded persons. We commented the results of these additional check for duplicates. In section 3.3, we concluded that we ended with an estimate of 77 to 188 additional duplicates on the Sarajevo killed list, which means that there is no more than 5 per cent duplicates left still in the list. And for the wounded person, the percentage was only 1 per cent, even less than four killed persons. So, this fraction of possible duplicates still present in the lists that we are touched with the major, with the report. This low per cent, in my view, low per cent of possible duplicates, means that the results that we discussed in the report wouldn't change significantly, once these additional duplicates would be excluded from the analysis. So, if someone would like to redo the analysis, but first of all, exclude the possible duplicates, the results would largely remain the same as we discussed -- as they are now in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell us what were the most important results or findings that you made in respect of casualties within the siege lines of Sarajevo during the indictment period?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I would like then to refer to the report itself, to the executive summary --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And please go a little bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I am sorry, I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Section 1, executive summary, table 1. On page 3. In this table we show the major finding of our study. We show the findings for the killed and wounded persons, separately. We show statistics that are related to all casualties. This is the first part of the table, the part on page 3. And on page 4, we include an additional small table, in which we show statistics related to a civilian casualties only. So it is just a continuation. The part on page 4, is a continuation of table 1 from page 3. What is really essential in this table, I am not going to discuss every single number in this table, I would like to summarise the major findings, really the most important findings only. We obtained for killed, 3.798 killed persons. This number are all casualties, civilians and soldiers. If we speak about civilians, then on page 4, we see the total number of civilians are killed during the indictment period, in the area within the front lines. We see the number 1.399. We then see that there were 670 women among those killed. I am speaking now about all killed. Civilians and soldiers. 670 women. And then 295 children at age from birth until age 17. I am still on page 3, first part of the table. I am looking at age now. At age interval 0 to 17 years, we see the number of 295 children. And we also see here 85 elderly persons, at age 70 or more years. So which gives quite a high number of casualties that are the most vulnerable groups, say, in the society. The same numbers for civilians are women 617, 617. I am now on page 4. The addition of the continuation of table 1 on this page. 617 women. If we still remember the number 670, all women killed, and now we are seeing 617 civilians. So this mean simply almost all women killed were just civilians. If we move now to the age groups and look at age 0 to 17 years, we see the number 267 children. 267. It used to be -- it is 295 for all children killed and 267 children civilians. It is sometimes the case that a child age 17 is reported as a soldier. I will explain later how it is possible that children, also children at that young age can -- were reported in different places as soldiers. If we look at age 70 plus, we see that there were 83 elderly persons, civilians killed during the siege. Next information, important information included in table 1 is the year of event. We see events grouped by calendar year. We have totals reported for 1992, 1993, and 1994. 1992 is actually not a full year. 1994 is not a full year either. 1994 is only represented by four months. It is September -- starting September. And 1994 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, which number is represented by four months starting -- which year?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: 1992, Four months: September, October, November and December. 1993 is a full year, all 12 months, and 1994 is the period from January to August. Again, it is not a complete year. So if we recalculate the numbers reported in table 1 and show the numbers as daily numbers or monthly numbers, for 1993, we obtain 11 casualties were day. This figure can be found in our report on page -- on page 27 in table 5. Page 27, table 5, in the second part of this table, daily numbers of casualties, we see for 1992 the figure 10.48 which is approximately 11 casualties per day. For 1993, we see 5.71 casualties, approximately six per day. And for 1994, two casualties 2.09, it is approximately two casualties per day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you observe that it is noted below there that in 1994, June is the last month included?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. June is the last month included because in July and August, the reporting was very much incomplete. Most of the questionnaires were collected in the month of May and June, so it doesn't really make sense to include July and August while -- for calculating this type of means, average values for statistics like that. So the same pattern actually is seen in the same table 5, page 27 for civilians. Most deaths daily are observed in 1992, almost four per day, and 1993 is the second year, two per day, 1994, was the last, one person per day. We also were able to present information about causes of death. In table 1, page 3, we show - and page 4 for civilians - we show cause of death. For -- I should explain the classifications of "causes of death" used in this report. Normally, in normal times, there is an international classification of causes of death of disease, causes of death, used in compilation of these type of statistics. This, of course, this classification, international classification of causes of death cannot be used in surveys like the Sarajevo household survey. Why? Because respondents who report causes of death, report causes death actually are very uncommon in normal times, and there is no codes for killing as such, conflict-related killing in the international classification, of causes of death. There are certain codes for violent deaths, but in no way normal people respondents participating in this survey are able to report proper cause. They just reported cause of death the way they saw it. So what they saw was, for instance, sniping or shelling or being killed by bullet from a gun. Or being killed in execution or they saw someone who died after being tortured. So this were the causes of death reported in the survey. There were also other causes, causes that are reported in normal times like accidents, different types of accidents, including traffic accidents, for instance. We tried to not to change the causes reported by the respondents. We tried to stick, as much as possible, to their reporting, especially regarding different types of firearms. Whenever shelling was reported explicitly as cause of death we kept this as a cause of death. Whenever sniping, again, we kept it as a cause of death. There were certain causes which were reported more specifically, someone -- there was a shooting and someone was killed in shooting. So in this case, of course, it is impossible to assign a cause of death like sniping or shelling. We actually invented a general category, other types of firearms, that was used in situations like this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you come to any ratio in respect to the civilian casualties and the soldiers during the period?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. We estimated that one civilian, but perhaps I would like to finish the causes of death first because I didn't mention the major results.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In table 1, we reported major causes of killing --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please slow, slowly if you can.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. In table 1 we report three major causes of killing. On page 3, 4, all casualties and on page 4, for civilians only. For all casualties, it is shelling, sniping and other firearms that were the three most important causes of death. We see the number of casualties who died because of shelling. This is 2.160. And altogether it is about 49 per cent of all those who were killed in this period. The 49 per cent is not discussed -- not shown in this table, but it is shown in the annex of this report, and more specific tables in which - and figures - in which we show these fractions. Sniping was the cause of death for 699 casualties and other firearms for 529. So it is sniping, 16 per cent of all casualties and firearms, 12 per cent. For civilians, the three most important, most significant causes of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What percentage of --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The percentage for sniping was 16 per cent and for other firearms 12 per cent, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am having a look at the cause of event at table 1 at page 3.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Oh, it is indeed I mentioned different percentages. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you put that table on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I have made a mistake. I was reading wrong numbers. So it is -- yes. It is this percentages that I was -- I should have referred to. I am very sorry. It would be for shelling 56.87. For sniping 18.40. Other firearms 13.93.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is in respect to the overall casualties?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you have the percentages in table 1 at page 4 --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: For civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- For civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At 66.62 for shelling and 18.08 for sniping?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, other firearms 7.22.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you or would you not say that the proportions of persons killed by shelling and sniping overall is quite similar to the proportions of civilians killed by sniping and shelling?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, it is for civilians, the fractions are at least for shelling, I see is 60 -- almost 70 per cent while for all casualties it is 57 per cent so it is a much higher fraction for civilians than for all casualties jointly for shelling. The second fraction is similar, the difference is minimal. The next one is other firearms higher for all casualties. But the first one, shelling, is significantly higher for the killed persons, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You had or I had asked if you had come to any conclusions in respect to the ratios of civilians killed and soldiers killed?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We estimated --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And wounded.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. The ratio of killed civilians compared to killed soldiers was 1 to 1.7. We discussed this ratio specifically on page 27 for killed persons. This is table 5. The ratio 1 to 1.7 is just an overall number. In table 5, we show ratios for monthly and daily casualties in every year of the indictment period for 1992, 1993, and 1994, separately. So the ratio is highest for 1992 in this table and for monthly numbers, it is 1 to 1.84 and for daily numbers, it is 1 to approximately the same 1.83.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: For wounded -- well, I actually didn't have the opportunity yet to say anything about wounded persons. The patterns for wounded persons are similar as those that I have discussed for killed persons. The numbers, absolute numbers are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem with the French booth, but, Ms. Pilipovic tells me that the Serbian booth is having trouble, and she is having trouble following it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was already listening to the French booth who seems to be able to follow you, which is a bit surprising. But the B/C/S booth seems to have difficulties. May I again ask you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am very sorry. We are speaking about ratios of between killed civilians and killed soldiers. I mentioned one ratio, which was 1 to 1.7. Perhaps it is also helpful to refer to table 5 to see exactly what I mean by a ratio of 1 to 1.7 or 1.8. Here we have figures that show us the ratio calculated using the monthly numbers, monthly number of casualties, and these ratios are shown here by year, 1992, 1993, and 1994. So for 1992, we have one civilian killed per every 1.84 soldiers. For 1993, we have one civilian killed per every 1.77 soldiers and for 1994, we have one civilian killed per every 1.24 soldiers. The results obtained on the basis of daily numbers of casualties are very similar. These are the results. I don't think we -- oh, yes, we discussed the ratio.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the wounded persons --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Wounded persons. It is now page 31 that I will be referring to, table 7. This table is exactly the same as the one for killed persons. The ratios are given in the last column. Again, monthly and daily number of casualties for every year, 1992, 1993, and 1994. And so we see that the ratios, although the numbers, monthly and daily, are much higher for the wounded persons than the numbers we saw for the killed persons. The ratios actually are similar. So for 1992, we see the highest ratio. 1 civilian per every 1.85 soldier and slower ratio for 1993 and the lowest for 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may take you back to table 1 at page 3 of the executive summary. In the middle of the page, you report the findings in respect to overall killed and wounded as a result of the -- or a reported in HSS94. And immediately below that you give a finding on the basis of an external definition in which the numbers of civilians are slightly higher and the numbers of soldiers are slightly lower. Could you explain briefly, if you can, the methodology behind that procedure.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: First set of figures, stated as reported in the HSS94, I am speaking now about this figure shown here -- I am sorry. This set of figures was obtained exclusively on the basis of responses from the survey. In the questions, I think 5 and 6 as far as I remember, 5 was the question in which killed persons were reported, and 6, wounded persons, there was an item -- a subsection related to the status of the person who was killed or wounded. The respondents had to report one of two categories, whether the person was a civilian or the person was a soldier. It was also possible that they indicated that they didn't know the status. This definition is used here as reported in HSS94. The respondents didn't have to prove to their interviewers the status of the killed and wounded persons. No documents were required, just self-reporting, status as seen by the respondents. We were in a situation that was, from our point of view, much better from the statistical, say, point of view, was much more reliable. We had at our disposal lists of fallen soldiers for -- from the ministries of defence in the Federation on Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska. These lists were complete. We have 28.000 approximately, names on the list from the Federation and approximately 14.000 names of fallen soldiers from Republika Srpska. The coverage of this list is the whole country, in both cases, the whole Bosnia-Herzegovina. By linking these lists with other sources with the census that we used in our project, we were able to compare those reported as soldiers, killed soldiers, fallen soldiers in the Sarajevo household survey and how they were reported on this official list. And this is what is meant here as external definition. For all these persons who had been linked, who have been linked the population census, we could check how were they reported and whether they were reported on the list of fallen soldiers. If a person was reported as a fallen soldier, we assigned the status soldier to this person. If the person was not reported as a fallen soldier, we assigned the state of civilian to this person. For the 20 per cent of those who were unlinked, approximately 20 per cent of the HSS population. Unlinked, we just kept the original responses from the survey. This resulted in new numbers of killed civilians and soldiers. We see that the number of civilians is higher and number of soldiers here is lower, compared with the previous definition. The differences are approximately 300, a little more than 300. We can check the differences specifically, I think in that report. Yes. It is on page 27, the second paragraph on top of the page, last sentence is reporting that the number of killed civilians is higher than previously by 333 and number of killed soldiers lower than previously by 319 persons. So the difference is between actually -- if we would only have two categories, civilians and soldiers, the difference would be exactly the same compared the previous numbers. But we also had a number of persons reported as unknown status by the respondents, and we were able to link these persons with the census we could add them by using external definition of status. So we ended with these two numbers, 333 and 319.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So tell me if I am correct, the 20 per cent where the status was unknown in HSS94, you linked that with the list of fallen soldiers produced by the government to come to the external definition?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Once again, I will say we linked 80 per cent of the respondents HSS94, Sarajevo household survey 80 per cent with the census. For those 80 per cent, we could compare whether they were reported on the lists of fallen soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So. If they were reported as fallen soldiers, only for those reported as fallen soldiers, on the official lists, we applied this category "soldier." For the rest we just assumed they were civilians, because they were not included in the official list of fallen soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is what we have done and this is the external definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask a question, Mr. Stamp, so that I perhaps do understand you better. If the official list which shows someone as a soldier that died, and when the household survey -- no, let me put it the other way. If the official list would not show someone as a soldier that died, and if in the household survey it would be indicated that that same person died as a soldier, would that mean that you would qualify him not as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. We would qualify this person as a civilian because that person was not reported officially as a fallen soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But whether he, in fact was a combatant or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a different story. We, in our report, don't use the term "combatant." We use the term "soldier" because we know how to understand this term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We don't know how to understand the term "combatant." In fact, in the survey, soldiers, the status of soldiers was reported. So we know that there were soldiers and civilians and it was the same of the official lists of fallen soldiers that were provided to us by the ministries of defence. Whether they died in combat as combatants is a different question. We don't have information to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have any specific information about the reliability of the registers of the defence, for the military authorities, as to who belonged to their armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that these documents are very reliable, the ones provided to us by the ministry of defence by both parties. Why? Because these were lists that were also used to provide families with post-mortem benefits, at least this is what we know from the authorities, from our meetings with the authorities there. So this list had to be reliable, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In section 7 of the report, you proceeded to estimate overall numbers of casualties. Can you briefly, if you can, explain, why was it necessary to proceed in that way?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The numbers discussed in the report in sections 1 through 6, were just aggregate statistics obtained from one source, main source, Sarajevo Household Survey. We, as I said, it is a large source, but it is incomplete and the numbers that we presented in our report are also incomplete. These numbers must be seen as minimum numbers, minimum means, at least numbers, and the actual numbers are lightly higher than that. Therefore, we decided in section 7 to present an estimate of the unknown overall total and this total is shown in table 18 on page 47. The method that we applied in this estimation is a standard method that has been used in statistics for very many years. It originally was used in estimating size of animal populations, populations that are difficult to count. So it was necessary to develop a tool that could be used for this type of situations. But it was many years ago since the first time this method was used for the first time. The method is described in details in the annex, annex number, I believe, 5 or 6. It is annex 6 in which we can find all technical details related to the method. In brief, the method is applied to, in this case, two samples, two sources of information. One source is household survey, 1994. The second one is the Bakija Funeral Home database. In the method, we analyse the overlap of the two sources and the nonoverlapping parts of the two sources, and on the basis of the analysis of these parts of the sources, we produce a number that gives us an impression of the unknown overall total.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you tell us what the unknown -- please -- I would prefer if you would not refer to that other document. Could you use the report.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And refer to the unknown overall total?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The unknown overall total reported in table 18, estimation was only done for killed persons. We didn't have sources to do the same for wounded persons. The overall total is 4.352.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which page are you at, please?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: 47, page 47, table 18. Once again, the estimate total is 4.352. All the groups are included in the estimation. We also show the ethnic composition of this overall total compared with the number, our number, obtained from Sarajevo household survey, that was 3.798. The estimated total is higher by 554 persons. And again this result must be seen as a minimum difference, at least 554 persons were killed in this period, in Sarajevo. And the reason that I am saying that this is a minimum number is that we only use two sources, one is Sarajevo Household Survey, second one is Bakija Funeral Home, but there are more sources and more records of killed persons that we have not included in this analysis. There were good reasons that we didn't do that. But, once we would include more sources and analyse more sources, the estimated overall total would be higher than what we presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Briefly, in respect to the date of event, death or wounding, can you comment upon the accuracy of the results in HSS94?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The date was carefully checked, we checked carefully, every -- perhaps not literally every date of event -- but when we started to work with this data, we made frequency distributions of every single variable in the database including the date of death for killed persons, for natural deaths, for wounded persons, date of wounding. And we looked carefully at the dates that appeared in the frequency distributions. We analysed dates that were outlined, that were irregular for some reason. Whenever it was possible, we corrected these dates because there were mistakes, evident obvious mistakes, entry mistakes, for instance. So the date, if unknown, incomplete, was -- or incorrect, was excluded from the database and the record was excluded from the analysis. But I understand that your question is rather related to the way dates were reported by the respondents? Yes. And it is, of course, difficult for me to make an assessment to what extent the respondents reported dates of events correctly. I believe that certain dates were reported slightly differently. There were shifts, probably, in terms of days, few days. Why? Because persons who reported these dates were relatives and people usually don't recall every date very specifically. So, there are perhaps differences between the reported dates and actual dates of certain events but I wouldn't expect that the differences are very large, like months or years difference. It would be very unlikely if we were to see this type of situation. I also believe that death is a very significant, very meaningful event in people's life. And they remember these type of events very well, and rather specifically. So I think that if there are differences, there certainly are certain differences. I wouldn't expect these differences would be significant and would change the numbers we presented in this reports. The timing perhaps could be slightly different, especially daily timing of death or wounding. But I don't think that the number, summary statistics that we discussed in this report, especially overall numbers would change dramatically, if we would correct the dates, somehow, in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may take you back to page 3 of the report. You were asked if the official list would not show someone as a soldier that died and if in the Household Survey it would be indicated that the same person died as a soldier, would that mean that you would qualify him not as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is on page 3, you said of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I was just putting the question you were asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
