utterances.text: If the official list would not show someone who was a soldier that died and if in the household survey it would be indicated that the same person died as a soldier, would that mean that you would qualify him not as a soldier? To which you answered yes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is that answer applicable to the 20 per cent which were not match to the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is not. The 20 per cent who were unmatched, are reported the same way as they are in the survey. So this remains exactly the same as in the survey. My answer only applies to the 80 per cent of those matched with the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that would explain the difference in number between the HSS results and the external definition?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just have a moment. Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. That is the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Stamp. Is the Defence ready to cross-examine the expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes indeed, Mr. President, however, considering how difficult this task is and how long it will be, we would like to ask for your leave, if we can do it as a shared task, half by Ms. Pilipovic and half by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber usually allows you to do so, under the conditions well known to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We could start now? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Madam Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam Tabeau, I am going to ask you some general questions to start with. What is a sniper?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I am not going to give you an answer, because I am not an expert. I am here as demographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. Thank you. You marked in your report, each time you marked a sniper shot, then killed -- there was other firearms or shelling. What allowed you, since you used percentages, to distinguish between firearms, other firearms and sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I tried to explain in this court that we tried to not to change the original responses obtained from the survey. So we just followed the original material and only, if there were small differences in wording, we actually recoded certain categories to obtain one the same name, shelling or sniping --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam Tabeau, I am sorry, I am going to interrupt you for quite a full time. Madam Tabeau, would you agree with me to consider that no one on your side checked if this was truly sniping or not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No one checked because it was impossible to check. It is the survey that is the source discussed in this report. And the responses are those from the respondents. So we never even tried to check whether it was -- what was a sniper, whether it was a sniping or a different cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam Tabeau, thank you. And if you can answer more slowly to start with, and briefly, but before the break, let us consider that the precise data that you give us, the figures that you give us, the sniping figures are random by necessity?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't think they are random by necessity. They are as reported, as perceived by the respondents at that time, the time the survey was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam Tabeau, if I define for you 100 cases of sniping and there were, perhaps, only 5 or 6 of them, technically speaking, and that you did not check that, would you still persist in saying that your figures are not random in their result?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I think that we are speaking about two different things. Randomness is one thing and about the other thing is whether one is allowed to change the original material. In my view, we are speaking about the second problem. We have not tried, at least, did our utmost best not to change the original survey material. And the figures in the report are as reported in the survey. And it is not about randomness, how respondents --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam Tabeau, I must interrupt you. Could you please repeat the question that I asked you, my own question that I asked you, could you do it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I can read it from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...100 cases. This was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes that was the question, without reading it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is time for a perfect break now is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was about to ask the court if they would not allow the counsel to argue with the witness, just to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think that's a fair observation. I have listened to the testimony of the witness until now. I have listened to your questions and I think there was no reason whatsoever to ask the witness to repeat your question, and I would insist that the Defence asks questions and not enter us into a debate with the expert witness. We will have a pause a bit later, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, did I understand you correctly if you told me, according to the either 61 per cent of sniping or 18 per cent of sniping, are you telling me that they are correct, absolutely correct, although you did not check, whether yes or no, this was truly sniping. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I am saying that based on the survey we obtained certain numbers of killed persons because of shelling, because of sniping. And these numbers are reported in table 1 in executive summary and also repeated in the text. This is all I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. But, Madam Tabeau, would you agree with me, to consider, yes or no, that if the figures you were given, for instance for sniping are false to start with, that obviously then can be concluded that your own conclusions would then be affected by those false results that you were given?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. This is also the case with every survey.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. But I just wanted to hear you say it. Madam Tabeau, I would now like to focus on an important matter. In this survey which is your principal source, there are two categories. There is a soldier on one side and then civilian on the other. We agree on that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You stated somewhere in your report that whoever was bearing a weapon would then be considered as a soldier. Do you remember that? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't recall how exactly I expressed my thought, but I was speaking, at least my intention was, about common way of or perception of a soldier at that time in Sarajevo. Well it is what I -- well, heard sometimes in -- from people in Sarajevo, that soldiers were just those who had guns and this is all I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Very well, Madam. Could you please remind me if you know, when did the war start in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, if you are going to obtain a historical testimony from me, this is, again, incorrect, because I am not a historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It is completely correct, Madam. Could you please -- I will tell you later why. Could you please tell me, when did the war start in Sarajevo? Could you please answer?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: You can refer to the report presented, historical reported by a historian, so I am not going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to ask for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you say it is beyond my expertise to answer to the question when the war started in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is not a field of demography, this is not a question for a demographer to answer this type of questions. This is why I don't want to give any answer on that, but this doesn't mean I have no idea. I mean, the war started in Sarajevo, but I think it is important that historians will define such dates and not demographers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, sometimes if you would have specific knowledge on that, which is not hearsay, for example, since you happen to be present at the first day of the war, then, of course it might be something that you are an expert witness. That means that you are, I would say, mainly answering questions as an experts. But if, by any chance you would have some specific knowledge as a witness, which, of course, can happen, then you should have to answer the question. So if you have any specific knowledge as a witness, I would like you to answer the question. If you say it is all hearsay and I am not in a position to analyse what I heard, not being an historian you are not -- I do not urge you to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can answer this question referring to the date that we discussed in our report. And I believe there were incidents in Sarajevo earlier in 1992 than from September 10, 10th of September. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we observe killed persons in earlier months, say starting in April. So this is what we see in the statistics from the survey. This is my answer. If we would define the beginning of the war as the day when the first person was killed, then I can answer this specifically by looking and searching through my database, when the first report -- death report was obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, could you please answer with a yes or no as much as possible, did you take into considerations these events, that is, the breakout of the war in your chronological tables?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I still don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I will rephrase it. Madam, did you take into consideration for your statistical calculations, did you take the beginning of the breakout of hostilities in Sarajevo, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: If we want to take a look at the earlier events, I must take a different document out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Tabeau, if you are using --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember, I don't remember when the first death was reported. If you want me to give a very specific answer I have to look for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing that I would like to ask you, is that if you consult any other sources, to tell us that you would have to consult that source and then, of course we will either -- we will then give a decision and it is clear for everyone then in this courtroom on what basis you are giving your answer. Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the witness has testified that by consulting some of the underlying data, that she would be able to tell you when, according to the methods she used, the first casualties occurred. Do you want her to consult these --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. What I would like, if that is possible, that the witness tells me, and I am surprised that she doesn't know it, if she can tell me now, how much would these facts, taking into consideration, that is, and Madam I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You gave two figures earlier and I marked them. This is 6.055 victims which is from the period from the 1st of January 1992, until the 30th -- let us say until September of 1994. And then you rectified this by a second list of data, by starting with the 10th of September 1992 and then you went until the 10th of August 1994, which is exactly the period that we are interested in here, and which comprises 3.788 victims or casualties. If my numbers and my figures are correct. Is that so, Madam?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well the numbers are not fully correct. But you are referring to table 2 and so you could have asked this question much more directly. I indeed indicated, a number, a large number of deaths in the period from January 1992 until the year 30th of September 1994. We can --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, very briefly, if my figures are incorrect, then I agree that this is 3.798 and not 3.788, but as for other -- the other figures that I quoted, 6.055, I believe that that is correct, that is one figure that I remember?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, these two figures are correct. Thank you. Now, I am going to come back to the first of these two figures, 6.055, which is a correct figure. This figure covers the entire period, that is included the period of January, February, March until September of 1992. We agree on that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Madam, did you make a statistical distinction between the months, January, February, March, and then months, April, May, June, Jul within the framework of this study, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The months, I mean, you mean 1992, February, March, April, May, June, July, 1992, these are the months?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Exactly and even January?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I didn't study these numbers because they were outside the indictment period. So it is not a report about the casualties of the siege as such --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam Witness, I am going to have to stop you. You just told me that the figure, 6.055 casualties or victims, is covering the period from the January 1992, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. So I am going to take this period from January 1992 until the end of August 1992, yes or no, could you please tell me, did you make a distinction between the first three first or even four first months and the following four months, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I didn't study these months from February until July in my report. I showed, however, the total for the period from January 1992 until the end of September 1994 in order to show how many records were excluded from my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, Madam. Thank you. I understand. Now, however, would you agree with me that if we consider that the war which is the case broke out about May 1992, and if we also consider there were fewer deaths in January, February, March, April, even early May 1992, compared to later when the hostilities started, would you agree with me to consider that the ratio of victims, the ratio of victims was a lot higher in the first -- the following three months rather than in the first five months of the year, that is, in June, July, August, even July and August 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I didn't calculate the ratio for the first months. So I cannot answer your question. I cannot compare because one part is missing, the ratio for the month February, March, April and April -- and May, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, would you agree with me to consider that the difference between the two periods that we are looking at, that interest us, that is, the period covering and the period for the figure 6.055 and the figure covered by the figure 3.798, and possibly some 2.007?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Something like that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are you saying yes?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think so. It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It is precisely 2.077. Now, would you agree with me, Madam, that this figure corresponds to about more than one-third than all of the victims that you have mentioned, that is the 2.0777 is equal to a little more than one-third of the 6.055?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if this would be a suitable moment, or if you wanted two questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, would you agree with me to consider that the third of all of the victims of this war happened in the period between the 1st of January and September 1992? Since we are talking about this?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you agree with me, this is my second question before the break, because in this first period, January to September 1992, only the months which followed the month of May, 1992, were the months of war, it was these months, these few months that they are the months which accounted for more than one-third of the victims that you counted in Sarajevo during your work; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, it is what you have proven already.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now the break can happen. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 10 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam expert, very briefly, would you agree in thinking with me that more people died during the war than people die in peacetimes, that seems to be obvious?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But I would also like to comment on table 2 that we discussed just before the break because I believe that you -- your understanding of figures in table 2 is not fully correct. So the conclusion we have drawn about the data --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you, Madam, if you don't mind. The conclusion I may draw is of no relevance. Figures are relevant and the figures will come on the basis of my questions. If your position was not right or that's important for you to explain, but my own conclusion is of no relevance.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So may I proceed with my explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I would like to explain to everyone in this court that in table 2, there are three types of figures presented. I am speaking about table 2, page 4. Thank you. We, first of all, present the general overall total. This is the complete survey material, this is 7.057 records. Then, we, starting from here, cleaned the data and carefully checked every single item by completing frequency distributions and eliminated from this database all records that were irrelevant to the period starting in January 1992 and ending in September 1994. The events reported, which remained in the database were still covering an area that is not the area within the confrontation lines. So in the next step, starting from here, 32.703 records, we eliminated from this total all events that were reported for the area that was different than the area within the confrontation lines. And we ended, for the period from September 1992 until August 1994, in the area within the confrontation lines, with this total and this number of killed persons. So the difference is not necessarily what you think that the difference between these two numbers of killed persons, 6.055 and 3.798, is related, first of all, to the period, but also to the area studied. And why the area of killed persons was different than the area within front lines. We should all keep in mind that Sarajevo, that there were huge population movements in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness explains at this very moment why one of the conclusions you have drawn in your question were not correct. And I think, if you draw these conclusions and ask for confirmation, that the witness could explain why they are not correct because we might have drawn similar conclusions. On the other hand, Ms. Tabeau, it is, until now you gave a clear explanation. If there is anything to be added, please do so. On the other hand, the Defence is under some time restraints, so in general, I would say, if they indicate that at a certain aspect they are not seeking any further information, then you would please follow the Defence. But, here, I think, if you want to finish or to complete your explanation, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was going to say that there were several thousands of displaced persons in Sarajevo who moved into the town and escaped the moment of the survey in the town. And these people reported killed in their families and these killed persons, of course, were not killed within confrontation lines, but in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, would you agree to say that the figures of 6.055 and 3.798 are right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: These figures are as obtained from the Sarajevo survey, so this is statistics from the survey.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Therefore, regardless of the population movements, you would agree in saying that indeed a good third of the casualties intervened in the period that is not covered by this trial, which is the period from January to late August 1992. Is this right or not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, it is not. Because for the whole conflict, sir, we estimate that the overall number of casualties more than 100.000. So this is irrelevant, how many thousands of killed persons --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I only talk about Sarajevo, Madam. And these are your figures. Okay, if I am not able to count, but your figures tell me this. We are not talking about hundreds of thousands of casualties. I am mentioning your figures, Madam. Am I wrong in counting the way I did and if I made a mistake, well, you have to prove it to me and if it is not the case, you have to conclude that my conclusions are right. Are they right or not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: They are not right. They are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Tell me.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The problem is that your interpretation of this table is wrong. I showed in this table why the total we reported -- the total of killed persons we report for the indictment period is 3.798. We obtained this total by adjusting the survey statistics and excluding a huge number of records to end with the proper number of killed persons. Your interpretation is wrong because you take the excluded records as the records relevant, somehow, to the siege of Sarajevo, which is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Madam, I'm sorry. Madam, could you explain to me the difference between the first column, that is, the column "All," and the other one, the following one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first column is a complete survey material. This is everything, everything that we obtained in our database after the computerisation of the survey material had been finished. This is all, entirely all what we had in the very beginning of our work. Starting from here, we cleaned the data, and very thoroughly, every single variable and excluded all records that were irrelevant to the indictment period and indictment area. And what I am showing in this table here, is a step that actually is irrelevant to the indictment period, and the indictment area as well. This is a period starting in January 1992 ending in September 1994, and the area that is covered by this statistics is larger than the area within the confrontation lines. So after excluding these records of those killed in different countries, for instance like Croatia, who died overseas, there were such cases. We ended with this total. These deaths and wounded persons were observed in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period January 1992 until September 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I am sorry. I still cannot follow you. The first column is the Household Sarajevo survey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The second one is from the 1st of January until the 30th of September.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Which is the difference between the two except that you clean up some things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were deaths and wounded persons reported in 1991, for instance, that is the difference. So it is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: In the first column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the first column, and there are no such events reported in the second column here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: And then between the second column and the third one is only the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Date and area. Two things, date and area of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I understand you well that from the first column to the second column, you would exclude all casualties abroad, that means, Croatia, Italia, whatever, but that it is still not limited to Sarajevo, there are still casualties in other cities, areas, municipalities, so it is not yet restricted to Sarajevo within the -- within the confrontation lines. And then to the third category, you corrected both as far as the time was concerned, as well as the geographical limitations of your research was concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is very correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least that I -- I hope I understand. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, if this is right, does this mean that all the graphs that you produced including the date of the 1st of January 1992 are, in part, wrong because inevitably they would deal with events that are outside Sarajevo. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Did I draw timing for all the months starting -- beginning 1992? I must check this because, to be honest, I don't see it here, at least not for wounded persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Fine. We shall check but I don't want to waste time. Now that we have understood this --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: See starting September 1992, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So they all start as of September 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Witness, let me go to other questions, issues of definition. Earlier, you mentioned the fact that you took in these definitions, sniping, shelling, other firearms. You indicated how you identified a soldier by definition. Going back, how far did the lists go in time, the army list.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't understand the question. How far did the list go in time, calendar time, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, if you --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... period?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I shall rephrase the question. So going back in time, you were given lists in 1994. Which period, which time period did they cover? How far into time did they go back?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. So I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I? I guess I don't understand it either and the witness seems to indicate that. Which lists given in 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness was about to answer the question. So it seems that after being reformulated, that she understands the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I want to be sure that my understanding is correct. I understand your question is related to the reporting in the survey, what period was reported by the respondents in the survey?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I try to -- I understood the question of Mr. Piletta-Zanin to be that when you received information of soldiers that had died, so that was information from the respective armies, how far these data went back? Were they from the 1st of January 1992 or from 1991 or? Well, up to how far they went back. Did I understand your question correctly? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As usual, perfectly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot -- I am unable to mention specific date when they started, but generally, the lists cover the conflict period, which I would generally mention as starting early 1992 until the end of 1995. So it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know when the army was created?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I think in the case of Sarajevo, I think you -- what you are probably thinking of is the Territorial Defence, that we didn't see army in the first months of the conflict, and Territorial Defence only. I have lists of fallen soldiers, official lists of fallen soldiers --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, I am sorry. Do try to answer my questions. If you don't know, just tell so. But do you know as of when the army was officially created?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before the army was created, there were indeed other structures. Could you tell us briefly whether these structures were the Territorial Defence, and on the other hand, the Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I certainly, I am aware of the existence of Territorial Defence in Sarajevo and of Civil Defence as well. But if you are asking me whether members of these two structures are reported in the lists of fallen soldiers, to be sure, I don't know, 100 per cent, I cannot give you my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. Madam, so it is theoretically possible, that members of, for instance, the Territorial Defence were not reported practically as such in the lists that were given to you by the government as being lists of soldiers, that is, of the soldiers who were in the lists of those killed in action?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is possible yes, theoretically speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mrs. Tabeau, we know that at the time, at the beginning of the war, there were very few uniforms, few distinctive signs or insignia, and I will take a specific -- I will give you a specific example. Let us imagine a civilian or an alleged civilian who is working near a confrontation line on a machine which could be -- on a field machine which could be worked by the army and this machine is targeted and the driver is wounded or shot at. This hit, this victim, is this particular person considered to be a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, it is not a question to me, but to the respondent who reported this death.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We can not distinguish between those who died in combat and not in combat and what is the meaning of combat. It is just how things were reported. This is what we showed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. When brings us to a question which Mr. President asked, there were only two formal distinctions, soldiers and civilians on the other side, but there was no way of allowing you to know if they were equally combatants. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Equally combatants --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am just talking about your report. Not your report, I am talking about the survey, the actual survey, the one that you call HSS, I believe, HSS94?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, if I understood you correctly, probably there were civilians reported as soldiers and soldiers reported as civilians in both ways of the survey. But for us who studied the responses only, it is impossible to assess what is the scale of these --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Mrs. Tabeau, would you agree with me in considering and I believe that this is obvious in your work, that there were many more victims, wherever they were, in 1992 than in 1994?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well generally for Bosnia, that is your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, Madam. I am talking about generally for your work, your work in on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think generally it is 92 in the relative terms, relative measures are telling us that casualties were more frequent in 1992 than in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, according to your figures s it true that we have an average of 10 casualties per day in 1992 on average, which goes down to two casualties in 1994 approximately is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Some approximate figures are like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, mathematically speaking, when General Galic took over the command and when he handed over to somebody else, that is in August -- from August 1992 -- September 1992 to September 1994, could we agree in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. considering that the situation was four times more dramatic in 1992, even five times more dramatic in 1992 than it was in 1994?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: These are the figures, but at the same time I must say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am objecting to the phrasing of the question as to what is more or less dramatic. Perhaps, it could be phrased a little more precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Casualties is considered to be dramatic by Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I will withdraw dramatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But that the situation simply presented five times more victims at the time that General Galic took over his command than when he handed it over.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The frequency is indeed as you said, how frequent the casualties were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. Madam, I would like to come back to the situation in 1992. Did you know, yes or no, whether in 1992 in particular was it difficult to tell apart on the outside between civilians and combatants, and I am talking about combatants, because in 1992 we don't have soldiers. So did you know that at the time?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: What do you mean by -- tell apart? Distinguish, this is the word?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes indeed, yes. Not how you could distinguish it, but did you know whether in 1992, it was very difficult to distinguish civilians from the military, speaking from a point of view of what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I read certain books and from the books I know that it was probably difficult. Probably, there are studies of this by historians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Now my question is whether you have included in your calculations any mathematical key which would allow us to take into consideration such probable error factor?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is impossible to take any measures to prevent from this type of situations. We even didn't have a question in the survey which would indicate the clothes people were wearing at the time, I think it is far beyond the survey question --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mrs. Tabeau. Therefore, the answer that I understand from you is that you based yourself 100 per cent on the figures that were given to you by the institute. Is that correct? And on army lists.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we studied the sources as we do with other sources and as we do always in statistics and demography. So I studied certain sources and obtained certain figures based on these sources and this is how my figures in this report must be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you have now approximately four to five times stressed again and again that if all women would have been reported as men, and if all men would have been reported as women, then, of course, the analysis would give a result which would not reflect the actual situation at that time, at that place. I think this has become abundantly clear. So please proceed, but try to avoid repetitious evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam you spoke of the institute which was -- which did the survey, but there is no name. Can you give us the name of the institute, please?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I believe the name is mentioned in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I know that it is in the report. But you, yourself, you did not state it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the evidence, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. We don't have to, otherwise the witness would have to read the whole report, which of course is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I insist, I insist, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... specific reason, but then not because it has not been pronounced, but because you have a specific reason for that. I do not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I insist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Piletta-Zanin, so I take it there is a specific reason why you want to know whether Ms. Tabeau knows by heart the name of this report or do you want her to read it from the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever she wishes. That does not matter. It is because I have questions to ask in relation to the institute which carried the survey out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the annex where the questionnaire is included on page 58, we read that it is translated title -- I am reading the English version, Institute for the Research of Crimes against Humanity and the International Law. That is the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Wasn't there another institute, Madam, which was called, the Institute against Muslim Genocide?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I mentioned this organisation. This is not a research institute, just an organisation, a group of people who was very active directly after the war, collecting information about victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I can conclude from this research institute's name that it was created ad hoc, that is, that the census was an ad hoc census that was taken?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: You are now speaking about the institute?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am talking about the institute on one hand, and the survey, the questionnaire on the other.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't think it is -- we can call this group an ad hoc group. It is a research institute that was created in 1992 and still exists today. And I don't think that this was an ad hoc survey. I would disagree, strongly disagree. I know that they have conducted several other surveys. This is just one of the surveys. I believe the largest one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Mrs. Tabeau, what was the objective of this survey? What was its aim of this survey, of this census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The objective was collecting information about suffering of Sarajevo during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And to be done what with?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This -- most people in this institute are historians. It was just for record, for history, not to be studied in reports like the one we made for this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you never speak about the objective, about the aim of this survey, of this questionnaire with the people who, let us call them, those who found the institute?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The founders of the institute, I didn't speak with the founders of the institute --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But those who fathered this research project, those who authored it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I did speak with the authors of the project and those who supervised the project and also involved in the project. And the objective, I mentioned to you, history, record, historical record is the one they mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I am going on to another line of questioning. In the questionnaire, in the survey, there are questions on the site of the incident, whether somebody was wounded or killed, that is, if they are injuries or deaths. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, yourself, or did you see these questionnaires with your own eyes; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The questionnaires, original questionnaires --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I have seen --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let us speak about the indications more precise of the locations, rather than the very general indications of the locations. Let us speak, for instance, like you give Dobrinja or Stari Grad. Are there more precise indications of the locations in question?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It was an open question in the survey questionnaire and the respondents were encouraged to report place of event, as specifically as they could. Mostly, they were able to indicate the local community where this event occurred. For our purposes, local communities are perfect way of reporting because these are small areas can be regrouped into municipalities and then we can show our results also from municipalities, as well as for the whole area within the front line control from the front lines. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: There were records where places were indicated more generally or more specifically than a local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But, Mrs. Tabeau, my question is the following: When you had these indications of the locations, of the sites did you try and create a subcategory, that is, locations that were very near military targets or positions held or combat areas?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I first of all, didn't try to recode the locations from the point of view from the military lines in Sarajevo. It was for me that I had a list of local communities, 89 local communities, that, for me, constituted the survey area. The survey -- the area was originally defined by the authors of the survey. So whatever population was accessible to the authors of this survey and interviewers, the population was questioned, and interviewed and we obtained responses from this population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, I apologise, this is just a question of a matter of time. Did you, yes or no, try to create subcategories, that is, injured near combat areas or military targets; yes or no? If you haven't done that, just tell us no.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Doctor Tabeau, if I -- and then I have to assume that your report does not take into consideration, therefore what we call in military terminology, "collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question would be, first, if you are talking about collateral damage, the first question would be whether any distinction would have been made anyhow between any justified military killing or wounding or unjustified. And when I read the report, such a distinction is not made. So if that distinction is not made, how could you even talk about collateral? So the proceeding question, I think, unless I am not correct in my understanding, Ms. Tabeau, but does not appear in the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But I just wanted things to be clear. Are we going on until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you asked for two to three minutes and I calculated another two to three minutes for the Prosecution. I see Mr. Ierace is coming in. So if this would be a suitable moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will continue for another two or three minutes with your leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I will come back to what we called the "duplicates," Doctor Tabeau. You tried to eliminate duplicates, but would you agree with me in saying that, among other things, to count deaths, if you have initial errors between civilians -- fighting civilians and fighting soldiers, then, of course, this would have an impact on the conclusions in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: What do you mean specifically? In every survey, there is a certain degree of wrong responses. But it works both directions. There is over-reporting and under-reporting. So it is -- I don't know what you want to know exactly. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I had in mind the fact that you did not have information on fighting civilians. In other words, if you lack information on fighting civilians, they are not to be considered as civilians or civil civilians, therefore this risks compromising the conclusions in your analysis. It is just a question of principal. Please do answer.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: At the same time I can think of soldiers visiting their families and being killed by bringing water. So this is what I meant by saying that is a certain misreporting. But this works always in both directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we can stop today at this juncture. We probably should resume tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau we have a few procedural issues to discuss and we have only 8 minutes left for that. So this would, for today, conclude your testimony. Mr. Stamp, Ms. Tabeau will be called, when exactly? Is it tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't looked enough through your new schedule. So we expect you to be in court again at a quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Ms. Tabeau, and the usher will now escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I inquire as the witness is leaving, so we can update our schedule, if we can be told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, asked for two or three -- yes, you asked Mr. Piletta-Zanin how much time the cross-examination would still take.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And how much time the court has made available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is there any idea on how much time the cross-examination in view of the Defence would take?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to check in a minute. We are going to have a look again at the questions put so far. We do not know as yet, but it is going to take some time, because we have several questions to put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me indicate to you that the Prosecution took two hours. I think two hours and two minutes. Perhaps three minutes. So could you -- if you could please indicate that at the end of this hearing, then now you asked for two or three minutes on another issue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. My firm received a phone call last Friday, Friday night, after the meeting. We wished everybody a good weekend. And we were wished a good weekend. And we were told that expert witness Kovacs was going to be heard again. I do not know whether this is an official decision by your Chamber, but I take it it is, in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is the decision of the Chamber that, well, there is perhaps a slight difference between the French and the English language. You are talking about "re-entendu" and I think the Chamber gave the message that the Prosecution could recall, that is of course the first step before you can hear again a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I take down that this witness might be called again to be heard again and this is the very reason why we want to address you now. First thing, we would like to receive a written decision from your Chamber so that we can look at it, and possibly seek an appeal certificate under Rule 73(B), I believe. Second thing, and we never had time to say so, in actual fact, we were never able to check the entire report. Never did we receive the entire report until last Friday, I believe. What I mean is, a report with its translation. And inevitably we are going to need some time to do all of this. Third thing, I am surprised to hear from the Prosecution that it has nothing to do with it, while anybody will see that if two documents bear different dates, in the original and in the translation, of course, we have nothing -- we don't have the same documents and we wasted a lot of time, not out of an error made by the Defence. And we would like to ask you as soon as we have a reasoned decision from you, because we had never received the documents before the date as is established by Rule 94 of the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know whether a response is really required, but without reiterating what I said last Friday, that explanation was given in closed session. I am happy for the hearing this afternoon to be in open session. I asked for closed session, so as to preserve the position of the Defence in any cross-examination they may wish to engage in with Doctor Kovacs on Thursday. Essentially, we are talking about an additional two or three pages which the Prosecution will propose to tender on Thursday, that is, the complete translation. I appreciate that the Defence submits that it has been disadvantaged, to some extent, by these developments, but by the same token, I think it is clear from the explanation that I gave last Friday, that, although this is of no comfort to the Defence, that it is not the fault of the Prosecution either. Naturally, we will do everything we can to assist the Defence in preparing itself for any further cross-examination that it wishes engage in on Thursday. I propose that on that day, Dr. Kovacs will simply be recalled, will, I anticipate, identify his full report and then he will be available for any further cross-examination that the Defence wishes engage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Without giving any further details at this very moment, we had -- the Chamber had hardly any opportunity to discuss the matter any further than last Friday when we communicated our decision that the Prosecution could recall the witness. I think that the Chamber will further consider the details of what has just been suggested by Mr. Ierace, whether that would be the course of action. But, at least, the Defence should prepare as good as it can, for a course of action as suggested by Mr. Ierace. That means that questions to be put to Dr. Kovacs on the missing pages, that that is one of the options that are there and of course that would be the option that would take most of the preparation. So apart from all the other legal issues, because we are very well aware of what the Defence has asked us, but we have to consider that, but if the Defence would at least prepare for such a situation, we will then further consider -- I think it will be tomorrow morning -- what exactly will be the course to be taken next Thursday. Perhaps even we would ask further comments from the parties for three or four or five minutes tomorrow. We have had no opportunity yet to discuss the matter in any further detail. But if the outcome would be that further questions may be put to Dr. Kovacs on the missing last few pages of the report, both parties, not only the Defence, but, of course, also the Prosecution should prepare for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very quickly. I am aware of time. But the Defence has to underscore that the first time when it translated the document into Hungarian, it focused on the conclusions. Taking into account the latest development, we will have to look again at whether the entire document matches in both languages, and this is going to take a lot of time. And that would be at the expense of the other cross-examinations that we have to conduct in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that you have a specific interest in checking whether the translation which is there is correct or not, and more special this time than you had at earlier occasions. That's quite understandable. We will adjourn until tomorrow quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 7.04 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of July, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 25
